title: 2-to-1 games with perfect completeness
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: The course is the start of an exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) of Khot's 2-to-1 games conjecture with perfect completeness: for every fixed delta > 0 it is NP-hard to distinguish 2-to-1 games of value 1 from games of value at most delta. The first lesson defines projection games, their value and their repetition, and builds the base game of the reduction (the manuscript calls it the source game): from a formula, a projection game of value 1 if the formula is satisfiable and of value at most sigma otherwise, with answer sets of sizes 7^t and 2^t. It rests on two theorems that are named hypotheses: a PCP theorem with perfect completeness and the parallel repetition theorem for projection games. The second lesson proves the inverse theorem for tables on matrices over the field with two elements: if a partial table often keeps its value under a random step of rank one, one of its values fills a positive fraction of a slice with a bounded number of row combinations and column values, with bounds independent of the number of columns and of the number of values; it rests on the expansion theorem for Grassmann graphs, the named hypothesis (GE). The third lesson defines the new game: the tree, the function spaces H_D (sums of spans of products of functions from the children), arrays and their joint function, the key of a function (the arguments it uses and its partition into fibres), and the constraints that forget one bit; it proves that every constraint has at most two preimages of every label and that a satisfiable formula gives a labeling satisfying all constraints. The fourth lesson proves the exact relations that every labeling satisfies (joint folding: adding products of rows at lower nodes to a row keeps the question and changes the restored values by the same products; the functional of a response on products of displayed rows), shows that changing one bucket of an array is a step of rank one, and defines the law of the tests: independent base questions at the leaves, a random path, recursive samples with products along the path, uniform arrays off the path, and a constraint at a random level of the path. The proof of soundness is not yet in the course.
prerequisites: finite probability spaces; Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form; the notion of a map computable in polynomial time

checks.reading: The manuscript 'Perfect completeness for 2-to-1 games' (OpenAI, 23 Sep 2026; eight sections, 188 KB of TeX) is being read; on 12 Oct 2026 Sections 1 to 3 (introduction, source games and inverse matrix structure, the tree of function spaces) had been read, with a first-pass check recorded in plan/OPENAI_105_SCOPING_20261012.md. Lesson 1 was written against Sections 1 and 2.1. Every step was derived: randomness does not raise the value; the conversion of the PCP instance to a 3-formula with three different variables per clause (bit coding with a default symbol, one clause for each rejected assignment, the chain of new variables for wide clauses in both directions, padding with all sign patterns), with the gap theta/(8B), B = 2^w max(1, w - 2); the value of the clause-variable game (1, or at most 1 - gamma/3); surjectivity of the positions; the base game with t from (1 - gamma_0^2/144)^t <= sigma. The exercises were computed by hand. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 2 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Sections 2.2 and 2.3. Every step was derived: the chart of graph subspaces and dim(L_M and L_M') = l - rank(M - M'); the two counts of neighbours ((2^l - 1)(2^m - 1) in the chart, twice as many in the Grassmann graph), hence retention at least eta/4; the interval as a slice (row combinations from a basis of A_0, column values from a basis of the orthogonal space of B_0); the lemma on dummy columns (the image slice, the extension L_0, the number 2^(dim W (dim D - rank d)) of preimages); the averaging over the values of the table; the erasure argument for good row fibres. The whole manuscript had been read once by then (plan/OPENAI_105_SCOPING_20261012.md). In the lesson the number of row combinations is called k, because a is also the vector of the step. The exercises were computed by hand. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 3 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Sections 3.1 to 3.3 (formal slots and pointwise spaces; joint evaluations and canonical questions; one-bit constraints and perfect completeness). Every step was derived: the properties of the spaces; uniqueness of the position of a reducible clause slot by surjectivity on pairs; the reduced domain and the dependence of the key on the relation of equal values only; the equality of the keys of f and of f composed with the projection; the constraint maps (onto, at most two preimages); completeness by the point given by a satisfying assignment. The lesson writes Theta_{D,a} for the quotient map (the manuscript writes Q_{D,a}) and 'key', 'label', 'restored value' for the manuscript's canonical key, legal label and restored output. The exercises were computed by hand (the dimension 13 in Exercise 6.1; the example of Exercise 6.2 is the manuscript's). No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 4 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Sections 3.4 and 3.5 (joint folding; joint evaluation of product generators; the distribution of tests). Every step was derived: the triangular shift is an involution of the space of joint values, hence the key is unchanged and the restored values are shifted; the functional b_y is the evaluation at a point that realizes the response; uniform buckets give a uniform array, and resampling the bucket of a gives the step M + a h with h uniform and independent; the sampler and the test law as in the manuscript (p uniform in 1..d, a_p uniform nonzero). The exercises were computed by hand. No discrepancy with the manuscript.

open_obligations: Not yet in the course: the soundness proof: the sampling comparisons (Section 4 of the manuscript), the two decoding steps (Sections 5 and 6), the clean repetition bound (Section 7), the choice of the parameters and the exact 2-to-1 output (Section 8). The main theorem is stated in the first lesson and not proved in the course. These sections were read once with a first-pass check (no error noticed); three places need a slow second reading before they are written as lessons: the inputs of the two decoders, the resampling lemma, and the local reconstruction on clean children.

Named hypothesis (PCP) of the first lesson: a PCP theorem with perfect completeness in the form of a gap for constraint systems of bounded arity over a fixed alphabet (Dinur 2007, as cited in the manuscript). Not proved in the course; the programme has no course on probabilistically checkable proofs.
Named hypothesis (PR) of the first lesson: parallel repetition for projection games with the bound (1 - g^2/16)^k (Dinur and Steurer 2014, as cited in the manuscript). Not proved in the course.

Named hypothesis (GE) of the second lesson: a set of vertices of a Grassmann graph over the field with two elements with retention at least zeta is dense in an interval of bounded co-order (Khot, Minzer and Safra 2018, as cited in the manuscript). Not proved in the course; it is the deepest of the three external theorems.
Relayed and not checked: the statements about the history of the conjecture and of the theorems (attributed to the manuscript in the lesson).
